# Git Merge vs Git Rebase

## What They Do

**`git merge`** combines two branches by creating a new "merge commit" that has two parents, preserving the exact history of how branches diverged and came back together.

**`git rebase`** moves your commits to a new base, replaying them one by one on top of another branch, rewriting history to appear linear.

---

## Visual Comparison

**Starting point:**
```
main:    A --- B --- C
                \
feature:         D --- E
```

**After `git merge main` (from feature):**
```
main:    A --- B --- C
                \     \
feature:         D --- E --- M   ← merge commit (M has 2 parents)
```

**After `git rebase main` (from feature):**
```
main:    A --- B --- C
                      \
feature:               D' --- E'  ← commits replayed, new hashes
```

---

## When to Use Each

### Use `git merge` when:
- Merging a **completed feature into main/develop**
- Working on a **shared/public branch** others are using
- You want to **preserve exact history** (auditing, compliance)
- Resolving conflicts **once** is preferable (merge commit handles it all)
- The branch history itself is **meaningful context**

### Use `git rebase` when:
- **Updating a local feature branch** with upstream changes
- You want a **clean, linear history** before merging
- Doing **interactive rebase** (`-i`) to clean up messy commits before review
- Working on a **private branch** no one else has checked out

---

## Key Tradeoffs

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserves exact history | Rewrites history (new commit hashes) |
| Readability | Can get cluttered with merge commits | Clean, linear |
| Safety | Safe on shared branches | **Dangerous on shared branches** |
| Conflict resolution | Once, in merge commit | Once per replayed commit |
| Bisect/blame | Harder to follow | Easier to follow |
| Traceability | Clear when branches diverged | Less obvious |

---

## The Golden Rule of Rebase

> **Never rebase a branch that others are working on.**

When you rebase, commits get new SHA hashes. If someone else has the old commits, their history diverges from yours and you'll create a mess when they try to push or pull.

```bash
# SAFE - rebasing your local feature branch
git checkout feature/my-work
git rebase main              # fine, only you use this branch

# DANGEROUS - rebasing a shared branch
git checkout develop
git rebase main              # will cause problems for teammates
```

---

## Common Workflows

**Keeping a feature branch up to date:**
```bash
git checkout feature/my-work
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main       # cleaner than merging main into feature
```

**Cleaning up commits before a PR:**
```bash
git rebase -i HEAD~4         # interactively squash/reorder last 4 commits
```

**Merging a finished feature:**
```bash
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff feature/my-work   # --no-ff preserves the merge commit even if fast-forward is possible
```

---

## My Recommendation

A practical rule of thumb:
- **Rebase** to incorporate upstream changes *into* your feature branch (keeps it tidy)
- **Merge** to incorporate your feature branch *into* main (preserves context)

This gives you clean feature branches AND a meaningful record of when features landed.
